title: RabbitMQ vs Kafka vs SQS
description: Compare the three most common message brokers across delivery semantics, throughput, and operational model.

data.text: RabbitMQ, Apache Kafka, and Amazon SQS are the three brokers most engineers evaluate when adding messaging to a system. Each makes different trade-offs between delivery guarantees, throughput, and operational responsibility. Understanding those trade-offs is the first step toward choosing the right one.

RabbitMQ implements the AMQP protocol and focuses on flexible routing through exchanges, queues, and bindings. It is ideal when individual messages need complex delivery rules, such as routing some events to one queue and others to many. Kafka is a distributed commit log that stores messages durably and allows multiple consumers to read at their own pace. It shines when throughput is high and replay is required. SQS is a fully managed AWS service with two flavors: standard queues for high-throughput, at-least-once delivery, and FIFO queues for ordered, exactly-once processing.

Quick selection guide
items: Choose RabbitMQ when you need complex routing, per-message priorities, or low-latency RPC-style request/reply.
Choose Kafka when you need replay, high throughput, or stream-processing patterns like Kafka Streams.
Choose SQS when you are already on AWS, want zero operational overhead, and can accept managed trade-offs.

data.title: Interview Tip
data.text: Be ready to explain that 'best' depends on the problem: Kafka is not always faster than RabbitMQ for small workloads, and SQS is not always the simplest choice when you need fine-grained routing.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: RabbitMQ excels at flexible routing and low-latency point-to-point messaging.
Kafka is built for high-throughput, durable event logs with replay.
SQS removes operational burden but locks you into AWS semantics.
No broker is universally best—match the tool to the access pattern.
data.takeaway: The right broker is the one that matches your throughput, replay, and operational requirements without over-engineering the solution.
